Commander of Iran's Quds Force from 1998 until his assassination by the United States in 2020, he was called the single most powerful operative in the Middle East — who was he?

Modeled on a notorious wave of Revolutionary France violence, this campaign of political repression and mass executions was carried out by the Bolshevik secret police during the Russian Civil War — what is it called?
Red Terror: Bolshevik campaign of political repression and executions (1918–1922)
The first Philippine president from Mindanao and the oldest to take office at 71, this former Davao City mayor led the country from 2016 — who is it?
Rodrigo Duterte: President of the Philippines from 2016 to 2022.
Captain of the Shinsengumi's third unit during Japan's Bakumatsu period, this samurai later worked undercover as a Tokyo police officer under the alias Fujita Gorō — who was he?

Beginning in August 1998, this conflict drew in nine African nations and roughly 25 armed groups after a Central African president turned against his former Rwandan and Ugandan allies — which conflict?
Second Congo War: 1998–2003 war in central Africa.
A viral video of him scolding sleeping city council members made this Japanese mayor an internet sensation before he placed second in the 2024 Tokyo governor's race — who is he?
Shinji Ishimaru: Japanese politician. Ishimaru ran in the 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election as an independent, but ultimately lost to incumbent Yuriko Koike.
Known as Madame Chiang, the youngest of a trio of politically influential sisters, she married a Nationalist Chinese leader and shaped his government's foreign relations — who is she?
Soong Mei-ling: Wife of Chiang Kai-shek (1898–2003)

After her husband was arrested ahead of Belarus's 2020 election, this activist entered the presidential race in his place — a decision the regime allowed, wrongly assuming a woman couldn't mount a real challenge — who is she?
In Greek mythology, this minor deity personified death itself, and was known to the Romans as Mors or Letum — who is he?
Thanatos: Ancient Greek personification of death.
Born Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, this British far-right activist co-founded and led the English Defence League from 2009 to 2013 — by what better-known name does he go?

Tommy Robinson: British far-right activist (born 1982). Stephen Christopher Yaxley-Lennon (né Yaxley; born 27 November 1982), better known as Tommy Robinson, is a British far-right, counter-jihad activist.
This Russian dissident and writer founded and chaired the Democratic Union party and sat on the editorial board of The New Times before her death in 2014 — who is she?
At 52, he became the youngest person to hold Vietnam's presidency since reunification, then resigned after just over a year amid an anti-corruption campaign — who is he?
Võ Văn Thưởng: President of Vietnam from 2023 to 2024.
As Lincoln's Secretary of State this anti-slavery Republican steered Union diplomacy through the Civil War and negotiated the treaty to buy the Alaska Territory — who is he?
After defeating his half-brother Sviatopolk in a war for the throne, this son of Vladimir the Great ruled Kiev from 1019 to 1054 — who was he?
Yaroslav the Wise: Grand Prince of Kiev from 1019 to 1054.

The first woman and youngest person ever to hold Slovakia's presidency, this lawyer and environmental activist won the 2016 Goldman Environmental Prize for fighting a toxic landfill in her hometown. Who is she?
Zuzana Čaputová: President of Slovakia from 2019 to 2024.
Who among these was born first?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?

Sergei Krikalev (born 1958) is the earliest of the four. Sergei Konstantinovich Krikalev (Russian: Сергей Константинович Крикалёв; born 27 August 1958) is a Russian mechanical engineer and former cosmonaut.
Which of these was founded earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these was founded earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is a physicist?
Louis Slotin is a physicist. Louis Alexander Slotin ( SLOHT-in; 1 December 1910 – 30 May 1946) was a Canadian physicist and chemist who took part in the Manhattan Project.
Which of these is a chemist?
Elizabeth Rona is a chemist. Elizabeth Rona (20 March 1890 – 27 July 1981) was a Hungarian nuclear chemist, known for her work with radioactive isotopes.
What is the atomic number of Tennessine?
Tennessine is a synthetic element; it has symbol Ts and atomic number 117.
What is the atomic number of Astatine?
Astatine is a chemical element; it has symbol At and atomic number 85.
In what year was Bill Wyman born?
Bill Wyman: William George Wyman (né Perks; born 24 October 1936) is an English musician who was the bassist of the rock band the Rolling Stones from 1962 to 1993.
In what year was Ferdinand Porsche born?
Ferdinand Porsche (3 September 1875 – 30 January 1951) was an Austrian-German automotive engineer and founder of the Porsche AG.
In what year did Pythagoras die?
Pythagoras: Pythagoras of Samos (Ancient Greek: Πυθαγόρας; c. 570 – c. 495 BC) was an ancient Ionian Greek philosopher, polymath, and the eponymous founder of Pythagoreanism.
In what year did Richard Feynman die?
Richard Feynman: Richard Phillips Feynman (May 11, 1918 – February 15, 1988) was an American theoretical physicist.
In what year was Molybdenum discovered?
Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.
In what year was Titanium discovered?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
Mikoyan MiG-27: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. It is based on the Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-23 fighter aircraft, but optimised for air-to-ground attack.
In which country is Dassault Rafale based?
Dassault Rafale: France. Dassault built a technology demonstrator that first flew in July 1986 as part of an eight-year flight-test programme, paving the way for approval of the project.
Who is credited with discovering Technetium?
Technetium: Emilio G. Segrè. Technetium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tc and atomic number 43.
Who is credited with discovering Cell theory?
Who is credited with discovering Hydrazine?
Hydrazine: Hermann Emil Fischer. Hydrazine is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula N2H4.
Sharing the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physics for unifying the weak and electromagnetic forces, who became the first Muslim scientist to win a Nobel?
Abdus Salam (29 January 1926 - 21 November 1996) was a Pakistani theoretical physicist and Nobel laureate.

Born into a prominent Stockholm family, this fluent-in-six-languages inventor filed his first patent at 24 and went on to hold 355 in all, while owning the arms-and-engineering firm Bofors. Who was he?
Alfred Nobel (noh-BEL; 21 October 1833 - 10 December 1896) was a Swedish chemist, inventor, engineer, and businessman.
Its scientific name translates roughly to 'fused lizard,' and it may be the largest of its armored kind at up to 8 tons — which dinosaur genus?
Ankylosaurus is a genus of armored dinosaur. It was named by Barnum Brown in 1908; it is monotypic, containing only A. magniventris.
Four novels and fifty-six short stories about a certain consulting detective made his name — but this knighted British writer-physician also invented Professor Challenger. Who was he?
Arthur Conan Doyle (22 May 1859 - 7 July 1930) was a British writer and physician.
Not contagious and believed to be partly genetic, this multi-system inflammatory condition can also cause blood clots, aneurysms, or blindness in severe cases — which condition?
Behçet's disease (BD; sometimes written Behcet) is a type of inflammatory disorder which affects multiple parts of the body.
Born as Hughes Helicopters' Model 77 to replace the AH-1 Cobra, this twin-turboshaft attack helicopter packs a 30 mm chain gun and Hellfire missiles in a tandem cockpit — what is it?
Boeing AH-64 Apache (-) is an American twin-turboshaft attack helicopter with a tailwheel-type landing gear and a tandem cockpit for a crew of two.
This basic unit of digital information most often consists of eight bits, and is called an 'octet' in network protocol documents to avoid ambiguity. What is it?
Byte is a unit of digital information that most commonly consists of eight bits.
Combining science, aesthetics, and technique, this field is the study and practice of making and using maps to communicate spatial information — what field is it?

Cartography is the study and practice of making and using maps. The fundamental objectives of traditional cartography are to:

Set the map's agenda and select traits of the object to be mapped.
Besides identifying the laws of elastic collision, this Dutch polymath studied Saturn's rings and improved the design of the telescope — who is he?
Christiaan Huygens (14 April 1629 - 8 July 1695) was a Dutch mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and inventor who is regarded as a key figure in the Scientific Revolution.
Scholars still argue whether it merely transmits meaning or also creates it, but the simplest definition of this concept is the transmission of information — what is it?
Communication is commonly defined as the transmission of information.
Grown from tubers and known by the folk name 'sowbread,' this Primulaceae genus features flowers with distinctively upswept petals — which plant genus?
Cyclamen is a genus of 25 species of perennial flowering plants in the family Primulaceae.
This Russian chemist's great law let him predict three undiscovered elements — germanium, gallium, and scandium — and a synthetic element now bears his name; who was he?
In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, honored for her analysis of how communities govern shared commons — which political economist was she?

Elinor Ostrom (ne Awan; August 7, 1933 - June 12, 2012) was an American political scientist and political economist whose work was associated with New Institutional Economics and the resurgence of political economy.
This ground-nesting songbird of Europe and the Palearctic sings its signature tune while hovering high over farmland and heath, and now also breeds in Australia and Hawaii — what is it?
Eurasian skylark (Alauda arvensis), commonly referred to in Europe as the lark, is a passerine bird in the lark family, Alaudidae.
Madagascar's largest carnivore, this slender, long-tailed mammal evolved cougar-like features independently and climbs trees head-first thanks to flexible ankles — what is it?
Fossa (animal) (Cryptoprocta ferox; FOSS- or) is a slender, long-tailed, cat-like mammal that is endemic to Madagascar.
The largest of four living anteater species, this terrestrial mammal of Central and South America is known for its elongated snout, bushy tail, and long foreclaws. What is it?
Giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is an insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America.
A retrovirus that gradually dismantles the human immune system, it leads to AIDS and, untreated, shortens life by roughly a decade — what is it?
HIV (HIVs) are two species of Lentivirus (a subgroup of retrovirus) that infect humans.

Often called the "father of the Indian nuclear programme," this theoretical physicist founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and the research centre later renamed in his honour. Who was he?
Homi J. Bhabha (30 October 1909 - 24 January 1966) was an Indian nuclear theoretical physicist who is widely credited as the "father of the Indian nuclear programme".

Forming at or below zero degrees Celsius, this naturally occurring crystalline solid is technically classified as a mineral and appears on Earth, other planets, and even in interstellar space — what is it?
Ice is water that is frozen into a solid state, typically forming at or below temperatures of 0 C, 32 F, or 273.15 K.
This Brussels chemist ran a famous five-year willow tree experiment and coined the word 'gas' from the Greek for chaos — who was he?
Jan Baptist van Helmont (12 January 1580 - 30 December 1644) was a chemist, physiologist, and physician from Brussels.
Cousin to the wallaby and wallaroo in the family Macropodidae, this Australian marsupial's biggest member is the red one. What is it?
Kangaroo are marsupials from the subfamily Macropodinae (macropods, meaning "large foot").

Seen using a silver stain and grown on media containing the amino acid cysteine, this genus of bacteria causes a severe pneumonia-like illness as well as a milder flu-like illness called Pontiac fever — name the genus?
Legionella is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria that can be seen using a silver stain or grown in a special media that contains cysteine, an amino acid.

Ranging across Eurasia with plumage of black, white, pink, and grey, this small insectivorous bird forms compact family flocks of six to seventeen outside the breeding season, its northern subspecies sporting all-white heads — which bird?
Long-tailed tit (Aegithalos caudatus) is a common bird species belonging to the bushtit family found throughout Eurasia.

Dubbed "sea locusts" by the ancient Assyrians and "prawn killers" elsewhere, these burrow-dwelling marine crustaceans are among the top predators of tropical shallows — yet they remain poorly understood. What are they?
Mantis shrimp are carnivorous marine crustaceans of the order Stomatopoda (from Ancient Greek (stma) 'mouth' and (pos) 'foot').
Used to treat cancers, autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, and even ectopic pregnancies, this chemotherapy drug and immune suppressant can be taken either orally or by injection — name it?
Methotrexate is a chemotherapy agent and immune-system suppressant.
Sitting just above the lip and under the nose, this style of facial hair on men has come in countless shapes across the centuries — what's it called?
Moustache is a growth of facial hair grown above the upper lip and under the nose of men.
This form of vitamin B3 is taken orally to treat pellagra without the skin-flushing side effect of niacin, and used as a cream to fight acne and reduce signs of aging skin — what's the compound?
Nicotinamide (INN, BAN UK) or niacinamide (USAN US) (IUPAC name: 3-pyridinecarboxoamide) is a form of vitamin B3 found in food and used as a dietary supplement and medication.

These pouched mammals originated in South America and crossed into the north during the Great American Interchange; one species is so common in the U.S. that people just call it a 'possum.' What is it?
Opossum are members of the marsupial order Didelphimorphia endemic to the Americas.
He co-founded Microsoft with his childhood friend Bill Gates in 1975, then stepped back from daily work in 1983 after a lymphoma diagnosis and founded Vulcan Inc. with his sister — who was he?
Paul Allen (January 21, 1953 - October 15, 2018) was an American businessman, computer programmer, and investor.

First described in 1850, this family of over 2,000 araneomorph spiders includes the cellar spider and the "vibrating spider" — and lends the nickname "daddy long-legs" to one of its species; what is the family?
Pholcidae are a family of araneomorph spiders. The family, first described by Carl Ludwig Koch in 1850, is divided into 94 genera.

First domesticated by ancient peoples of the Iranian plateau roughly 5,000 years ago, this deciduous shrub bears a fruit rich in symbolic and mythological meaning across many cultures — name the fruit?
Pomegranate (Punica granatum) is a fruit-bearing, deciduous shrub in the family Lythraceae, subfamily Punicoideae, that grows to between 1.5-5 metres (5-16 ft) tall.
Ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius believed this oratorical skill could profoundly move even those not present in the room — what is the term for addressing a live audience?
Public speaking is the delivery of a speech to a live audience.
Derived from an Ancient Greek word for 'flow,' this umbrella term covers more than 200 different conditions causing chronic joint or connective-tissue pain, including arthritis — what's the term?
Rheumatism (from the Ancient Greek, rhema) or rheumatic disorders are conditions causing chronic, often intermittent pain affecting the joints or connective tissue.
After dropping out of Stanford and co-founding a startup later sold for over $40 million, this entrepreneur led Y Combinator before taking the helm of a leading AI company — who is he?
Sam Altman (born April 22, 1985) is an American entrepreneur and investor who has been the chief executive officer (CEO) of the artificial intelligence company OpenAI since 2019.

This dog breed from southern China, traditionally kept as a property guardian, was driven to the brink of extinction in the 20th century and is known in the West for its deep wrinkles. What breed is this?

Shar Pei (Cantonese; pinyin: sh p) is a dog breed from
southern China.
This family of roughly 1,450 moth species, with narrow wings and streamlined bodies built for fast, hovering flight, are so nimble they're routinely mistaken for hummingbirds — what are they called?
Sphingidae are a family of moths commonly called sphinx moths, also colloquially known as hawk moths, with many of their caterpillars known as hornworms.

Which British single-seat fighter plane, the only such aircraft Britain produced continuously throughout World War II, was famous for its innovative elliptical wing designed to be as thin as possible?
Supermarine Spitfire is a British single-seat fighter aircraft that was used by the Royal Air Force and other Allied countries before, during, and after World War II.
Used to treat asthma and COPD, this methylxanthine drug — a cousin of caffeine — turns up in trace amounts in tea, chocolate, and yerba mate. What is it?
Theophylline is a drug that inhibits phosphodiesterase and blocks adenosine receptors.
Named for the compulsive pulling of one's own hair, this disorder brings a brief positive feeling with each pull but is notoriously hard to stop — what is it?
Trichotillomania (TTM), also known as hair-pulling disorder or compulsive hair pulling, is a mental disorder characterized by a long-term urge that results in the pulling out of one's own hair.
This broad category of creative disciplines spans painting, sculpture, photography, and architecture, and includes applied fields like industrial and fashion design — what do we call it?
Visual arts are art forms such as painting, drawing, printmaking, sculpture, ceramics, photography, video, image, filmmaking, design, crafts, and architecture.
This mosquito-borne viral disease causes chills, nausea, and muscle pain, and in about 15% of cases progresses to liver damage that turns the skin a telltale color — what disease is it?
Yellow fever is a viral disease of typically short duration.
This class of bony fish accounts for nearly 99% of all living fish species, ranging in size from an 8-millimeter minnow to a giant sunfish weighing 2,700 kilograms — what is it?
Actinopterygii: Class of ray-finned bony fishes.
Its very name comes from the Arabic for 'the kohl,' and chemically it's any compound carrying a hydroxyl group on a saturated carbon — a family that ranges from methanol to cholesterol. What is it?
Alcohol (chemistry): Organic compound with at least one hydroxyl (–OH) group.
This functional group, formed by replacing a carboxylic acid's hydroxyl with an amino group, creates the peptide bonds that link amino acids into proteins — what is it?
Amide: Organic compounds of the form RC(=O)NR′R″.
Belonging to the suborder Vermilingua and closely related to sloths, these mammals include giant, silky, and tamandua species that feed almost exclusively on ants and termites — what are they called?
Anteater: Mammals known for eating ants and termites.
Some 1,800 years before Copernicus, this ancient Greek astronomer placed the Sun at the center of the universe and argued it was just another star — who was he?
Aristarchus of Samos: Greek astronomer and mathematician (c. 310 – 230 BC)
Native to tropical Southeast Asia, this small tree bears bell-shaped rose-to-purple flowers and a ridged fruit that forms star-shaped slices when cut crosswise — which species?
Averrhoa carambola: Species of tree. It is a small tree or shrub that grows 5 to 12 m (16 to 39 ft) tall, with rose to red-purple flowers.

Nicknamed 'Huey,' this American utility helicopter became the first turbine-powered rotorcraft in U.S. military service, developed in the 1950s to meet an Army need for medical evacuation and utility missions. Which aircraft?
Bell UH-1 Iroquois: Huey family of American military utility helicopters.
This organ stores urine received from the kidneys via the ureters before it exits through the urethra, and gives us the medical term 'cystitis' when inflamed — what is it?
Bladder: Organ in vertebrates that collects and stores urine from the kidneys before disposal.
Named from Greek words for 'slow' and 'heart,' this condition means a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute — sometimes normal in well-conditioned athletes — which condition?
Bradycardia: Heart rate below the normal range.
Common in cancer, heart failure, and other serious illnesses, this syndrome causes muscle wasting that better nutrition alone can't reverse — what is it?
In 1886 this German engineer patented what's considered the first practical automobile, and his Mannheim company later merged with Daimler — who is he?
Carl Benz: German designer and engineer (1844–1929)
Documented anatomically since the time of Hippocrates over 2,000 years ago, this roughly 4-centimeter-long fibromuscular organ connects the vagina to the uterine cavity. What structure is this?
Cervix: Lower part of the uterus in the female reproductive system.
This complex of DNA and histone proteins packages long strands of genetic material into compact structures while controlling access for transcription, replication and repair — what is it?
Chromatin: Complex of DNA and protein in eukaryotic cells.
This genus of demersal fish, named by Linnaeus in 1758, includes an Atlantic and a Pacific species prized for their mild flavor and flaky white flesh — what fish is it?
Cod: Common name for several fish, but mainly the demersal genus Gadus.
With a long hooked bill and webbing between all four toes, this fish-eating aquatic bird family includes the 'great' species commonly seen around Britain and Ireland — what are they called?
Cormorant: Family of aquatic birds. The common names "cormorant" and "shag" have been assigned to different species in the family somewhat haphazardly.
Sometimes called 'bipolar III,' this mood disorder involves cycling periods of mild depression and elevated mood that never reach the severity of full manic or depressive episodes — what is it?
Cyclothymia: Mental disorder. Cyclothymia differs from bipolar disorder in the fact that major depression and mania are not found.
Whether for an object, a process, or a system, this is the intentional concept or proposal created by a thinking agent, balancing purpose, aesthetics, and constraints — what single word names it?
Design: Plan for the construction of an object or system.
Brought to Australia as an infant, this geologist joined Shackleton's Nimrod Expedition and became a leading figure of the Heroic Age of Antarctic exploration — who is it?
Douglas Mawson: Australian geologist and explorer of the Antarctic (1882–1958)

Carried out mainly at power plants, this process transforms heat from burning fuel or nuclear fission — or the motion of water and wind — into power used by homes and businesses. What is this process called?
Electricity generation: Process of generating electrical power.
He coined the term 'quantum entanglement' in 1935 and shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac for his work on atomic theory — who is he?

Native to a huge swath of Eurasia but declared a noxious species in New South Wales after damaging native fish, this predatory freshwater game fish is known locally in Australia as 'redfin' — which fish?
The discipline that studies money, currency, assets, and liabilities, divided into personal, corporate, and public branches — what is this field of study called?
Finance: Academic discipline studying businesses and investments.

Coated in cornmeal and pan-cooked while still unripe, this dish was originally a Northeastern and Midwestern staple before a hit movie rebranded it as quintessentially Southern comfort food — what is it?
Fried green tomatoes: American dish. Fried green tomatoes is a culinary dish usually found in the United States, made from unripe (green) tomatoes coated with cornmeal and fried.

Germany's first professor of experimental physics is remembered both for the tree-like electrical discharge patterns named after him and for the witty posthumous notebooks he called "waste books" — who was he?
Georg Christoph Lichtenberg: German scientist and satirist (1742–1799)
Known online by the alias 'anakata,' this Swedish computer specialist co-founded a notorious BitTorrent site and later helped WikiLeaks with its 2010 release of a leaked military video — who is he?
Gottfrid Svartholm: Swedish computer specialist. Parts of an interview with Svartholm commenting on the May 2006 police raid of The Pirate Bay are featured in Good Copy Bad Copy and Steal This Film.
Nicknamed the slime eel, this jawless marine scavenger is the only living animal with a skull but no proper backbone — what is it?
Hagfish: Class of eel-shaped, slime-producing animal.

Governed by rules laid out in a document called a blazon, this medieval discipline of coats of arms, crests, and mottoes may have arisen so knights could recognize commanders behind their helmets — what is it?
Heraldry: Discipline of the design and study of coats of arms.
Running from your shoulder to your elbow, this long arm bone has a constriction nicknamed the 'surgical neck' due to its tendency to fracture — which bone?
Humerus: Long bone of the upper arm. It connects the scapula and the two bones of the lower arm, the radius and ulna, and consists of three sections.

Trained originally as a naval architect before becoming a self-taught nuclear physicist, this scientist directed the Soviet Union's atomic bomb program and earned the nickname 'father of the Russian bomb' — who is he?
This tech entrepreneur co-founded Twitter, later built a fintech company behind Square, Cash App, and Tidal, and also helped launch the decentralized network Bluesky?
This English scientist's 1808 book, 'A New System of Chemical Philosophy,' laid the foundations of modern atomic theory, and he also kept daily weather records for over fifty years — who was he?
John Dalton: British chemist and physicist (1766–1844)
Patented in 1967 and approved for medical use in 1980, this propionic-acid-class NSAID works by blocking prostaglandin production — what is it?
Native to the Mediterranean and used to season food as a bay leaf, this aromatic evergreen prominent in classical Greco-Roman culture can grow up to 20 metres tall — what is its scientific name?
Laurus nobilis: Species of flowering plant in the laurel family Lauraceae.
Nearly always affecting women, this incurable condition causes fat buildup in both legs that's resistant to typical weight loss and often mistaken for other circulatory disorders — what is it?
Lipedema: Condition involving excessive deposition of fat in the legs.
The sole member of its genus in the soapberry family, this sweet, mildly tart fruit carries a distinctive rose-like aroma and comes in Indochinese, Philippine, and Javanese subspecies — what is it?

Often making people tall and thin with long fingers and very flexible joints, this connective-tissue disorder carries serious risks to the heart and aorta — caused by a mutation in the FBN1 fibrillin gene — which condition?
Marfan syndrome: Genetic disorder involving connective tissue.

Fever, a fierce headache, neck stiffness, and a telltale rash that doesn't fade when a glass is rolled over it can signal this inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord — what is it?

Meningitis: Inflammation of membranes around the brain. Meningitis (pl. meningitides) is acute or chronic inflammation of the protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord, collectively called the meninges.
Developed for the Soviet Union, this swept-wing jet fighter dominated early dogfights in the Korean War and prompted the US to rush its F-86 Sabre into combat — which aircraft?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15: Soviet fighter aircraft. The MiG-15 was one of the first successful jet fighters to incorporate swept wings to perform near Mach 1.

Prized by gourmet cooks yet toxic if eaten raw or undercooked, this genus of honeycomb-capped edible fungi is difficult to cultivate, making wild harvests a multimillion-dollar industry — which fungal genus?
Morchella: Genus of fungi. Morchella, the true morels, is a genus of edible sac fungi closely related to anatomically simpler cup fungi in the order Pezizales (division Ascomycota).
Sold under the brand name Revia, this medication blocks opioid receptors to reduce cravings in alcohol and opioid use disorders and is combined with bupropion to treat obesity — what is it?
Naltrexone: Medication. It has also been found to be effective for the treatment of other addictions and may be used for them off-label.
Discovered in 1846 by Ascanio Sobrero, this oily explosive liquid became the key ingredient in dynamite — what is it?

Sold under the brand name Zofran, this serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist prevents chemotherapy- and surgery-related nausea without the dopamine-blocking side effects that cause muscle restlessness — what is this drug?
Ondansetron: Medication to prevent nausea and vomiting.
Known for its fragrant leaves used to flavor dishes across Southeast Asia, Sri Lanka and Hainanese cuisine, this member of the screwpine genus is prized in many Asian kitchens — which plant?
Pandanus amaryllifolius: Species of tropical plant.
This bony ring connects the spine to the lower limbs at the hip joints, formed by the sacrum, coccyx, and a pair of hip bones — what body region?
Pelvis: Lower torso of the human body.
This colorless, highly toxic pnictogen hydride is pure when odorless, but technical samples reek of rotting fish — and impurities can make it burst into flame in air — what is it?
Named after a French mathematician and physicist, this materials-science measure captures how much a material bulges sideways when compressed lengthwise — what is it?
Poisson's ratio: Measure of material deformation perpendicular to loading.
Found just below the bladder with the urethra passing through it, this male-only gland acts like a muscle-driven switch between urination and ejaculation — which organ?
Prostate: Gland of the male reproductive system.
Sold as Seroquel and prescribed for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, this atypical antipsychotic is also widely (and questionably) used as a sleep aid for its tranquillizing effect — which drug?
Quetiapine: Atypical antipsychotic medication. Quetiapine is believed to work by blocking a number of receptors, including those for serotonin and dopamine.

This dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces predicts whether fluid flow will be smooth and laminar or chaotic and turbulent, and is used everywhere from pipe flow to aircraft wings — what is it?
Reynolds number: Ratio of inertial to viscous forces acting on a liquid.
Also called baked-apple berry or Arctic berry, this amber-hued fruit resembling a blackberry grows wild across boreal forests and Arctic tundra — what's its scientific name?
Rubus chamaemorus: Species of flowering plant in the rose family.
This large, rainbow-plumed parrot native to the forests of Central and South America is the national bird of Honduras — what is it?
Scarlet macaw: Species of bird. Like its relative the blue-and-yellow macaw, the scarlet macaw is a popular bird in aviculture as a result of its striking plumage.

Though crustaceans within this food category are more closely related to insects and spiders than to true fish, what group — including molluscs, crustaceans, and echinoderms — ranks among the most common food allergens?
Shellfish: Culinary and fisheries term for exoskeleton-bearing aquatic invertebrates.
Nicknamed a 'truth serum' in popular culture despite dubious real-world reliability, this fast-acting barbiturate anesthetic is marketed under the brand name Pentothal — which drug?
Sodium thiopental: Barbiturate general anesthetic. It is the thiobarbiturate analog of pentobarbital, and an analog of thiobarbital.
This English clergyman was the first person ever to measure blood pressure, and on the side he invented a ventilator and even wrote a tract against drinking — who was he?
Stephen Hales: English clergyman and scientist (1677–1761)
Commonly known as fainting, this fast-onset, short-duration loss of consciousness and muscle strength is typically caused by a sudden drop in blood flow to the brain — what's the medical term?
Syncope (medicine): Transient loss of consciousness and postural tone.
Patented in 1953 and originally derived from Streptomyces bacteria, this antibiotic treats ailments from acne to cholera to plague by blocking bacterial protein production — which drug?
Tetracycline: Antibiotic. It is available in oral and topical formulations.
